dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment

evidence.note: Opening is environment inventory (ls, python, pip, existing skeleton) followed by immediate coding straight from the prose prompt. No stripe SDK import, no doc lookup, no round-trip probe at any point — the entire Stripe contract is drawn from memory + prompt.

Builds the error-envelope exception classes, list envelope, and TEST_CARDS from recall; establishes core contract for main resources but never validates it against an external reference or the SDK's api_base/auth behavior (never confirmed).

Catches real Stripe-fidelity corners from memory: decline cards should be valid at PM-create and decline only at confirm; card number must be last4 not full PAN; charges must be a list-object not bare ID list. Self-correcting, but grounded in remembered Stripe behavior, not probed API.
Handles idempotency error-body replay (same request_id) and different-body 400 — the hard trap semantics — but again from prompt/memory rather than SDK verification.
Final verification is curl-only; the SDK the task centers on is never exercised, so no subsystem behavior is cross-checked against actual SDK round-trips.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reconstructs the core Stripe contract — error envelope, list envelope, test-PAN behavior, PaymentIntent state machine — and even catches several deep Stripe-fidelity corners (last4 sanitization, charges list-object, decline-at-confirm, error-body replay) self-correctingly, which is stronger than the 'half-guessed' level 3. But every bit of this comes from the prose prompt plus memory: it never uses the stripe SDK, never confirms how api_base/auth are set, and never verifies the PAN set or any subsystem against a real API/SDK round-trip, which is exactly what level 5 and above require. That places it at a 4 — solid memory-based contract recall without any grounded probing.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps

evidence.note: Consistent modular decomposition plan (config→errors→store→auth→idempotency→models→router); infrastructure/auth/idempotency built as distinct modules before resource routes, showing an ordered hierarchy rather than ad-hoc endpoint hopping.

Testing followed a deliberate risk-aware order and treated idempotency and PI state machine as distinct workstreams with explicit done-conditions: manual capture returns requires_capture, capture-of-succeeded returns 400, idempotency success-replay/error-replay/different-body-400 all checked individually.

First server boot only happened after nearly the entire codebase (all modules + all routes) was written — a big-bang build, so no early bootable auth'd skeleton was verified, which is what anchor 8 requires.

Webhook delivery (retry/backoff/re-sign) repeatedly placed at the tail of plans and never given its own explicit check ('verify by checking logs'); only 2 of the 3 named traps were ring-fenced with real acceptance conditions.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent demonstrated clear milestone structure (auth/idempotency infrastructure first, then resource groups, then a deliberately ordered test pass) and recognized idempotency and the PI state machine as distinct workstreams with explicit per-behavior done-conditions, comfortably exceeding the flat-checklist anchor (3) and satisfying the milestone+trap-recognition anchor (5). It falls short of anchor 8 because it never secured a verifiable auth'd skeleton early (booting only after building nearly everything) and left the webhook-retry trap as a perpetually deferred tail item without its own explicit check, so it lands at 6 — between anchors 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks

evidence.note: Boots server in background and smoke-tests health, auth-error, and empty list via curl — baseline active verification beyond 'code was written'.

Constructed targeted checks for two of the three named traps: invalid/decline card → 402 card_error envelope, manual-capture state flow, and capturing a succeeded intent → 400 payment_intent_unexpected_state.
Verified idempotency replay success, same-key-different-body → 400, and the hard cached-error replay (retry of a declined call returns the same request_id) — strong trap coverage.
Found a 500 in the permission middleware, fixed it, restarted and re-tested restricted-key read-vs-write 403 enforcement — a self-correcting verify/fix/re-verify loop.
Webhook 5xx retry/backoff/re-sign repeatedly listed as intent to 'verify in server logs' but never actually exercised; final submission asserts it works without evidence.
No occurrence of the stripe SDK or api_base anywhere — all verification is curl, so the SDK-round-trip requirement of the high anchors is entirely absent; concurrency/no-double-charge never tested.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent did far more than happy-path curl: it actively verified the idempotency traps (replay incl. cached error body, same-key-different-body → 400), the state-machine trap (capture succeeded → 400), invalid-PAN decline → 402, error envelopes/HTTP mappings, pagination, and restricted-key 403s — including a fix-and-re-verify loop, clearly above anchor 5. But it never used the real stripe SDK against api_base (a core requirement of anchor 8) and left webhook 5xx retry/backoff and concurrent same-key serialization merely stated-as-intent and assumed, so it falls short of 8. This interpolates to a 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface

evidence.note: Systematically walked each resource family (refunds, products/prices, subscriptions, invoices, events, webhooks, restricted keys) in sequence, each Plan re-listing what remained — a consistent running checklist across the wide surface.
Explicit done-vs-remaining summary: enumerated all working subsystems and flagged 'permission enforcement is missing' as the key open item — accurate coverage accounting.
Distinguished implemented-only from missing: noticed the permission helper existed but was never wired into routes, and reallocated attention to fix it rather than silently dropping it.
Comprehensive retest caught a missing webhook_endpoints update route and an incorrect charges field shape — evidence it kept re-checking coverage against the route table.

Declared task complete while webhook delivery retry/re-sign and the billing worker were never actually verified (only 'planned to check logs'); two trap subsystems silently absent from the final done accounting.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an accurate, continuously-updated checklist of all 12 resource families and generally knew what remained, catching missing pieces like permission wiring and the webhook-update route (well above the level-5 anchor). It fell short of level 8 because it never time-boxed or named the multi-step circling on permission middleware, and — most tellingly — it declared full completion while the webhook-retry and billing-worker traps were silently left unverified, a lapse in maintaining the whole-horizon coverage picture. This places it at a 6: strong running-checklist tracking with a real end-of-run gap.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures

evidence.note: Discovered test-decline PANs were wrongly rejected at PM creation; reframed as a contract-semantics error (decline cards are valid PANs, decline at confirmation) and revised the model rather than tweaking a symptom.
Found full card number leaked in PM response vs Stripe's last4; fixed and propagated sanitization across create and list endpoints — a fix applied to related endpoints, not just the one that failed.

Root-cause pass: missing _charge_from_pi, zero-amount manual-capture charge, and idempotency not caching error bodies were fixed structurally (idempotency error replay) rather than patched superficially.

Permission enforcement: multiple diagnosed iterations culminating in correctly identifying that Starlette middleware bypasses FastAPI's exception handler (500 error), then structurally pivoting to request.state auth + JSONResponse in middleware, re-testing after.
Noticed PaymentIntent.charges was a plain ID list rather than Stripe's {object:list,data,has_more} envelope and corrected the shape.

dimensions.reasoning: Across the horizon the agent repeatedly let contradicting evidence rewrite its design: it updated its mental model of the contract (test-PAN decline semantics, charges envelope, last4 sanitization) and propagated fixes across related endpoints, matching the level-8 anchor. It also performed genuine structural pivots with correct root-cause diagnosis (idempotency error-caching, the Starlette-vs-FastAPI middleware exception issue) while preserving verified work — touching level 10. It falls short of a clean 10 because the permission work showed some thrash before landing and the webhook retry/re-sign trap was never truly falsification-tested before it declared completion, so I place the observed level at 8.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that emulates the Stripe REST API at the wire level, faithful enough that the real `stripe` Python SDK works unchanged. Difficulty comes from breadth (12+ resource families, list/error envelopes, restricted keys) AND depth on three explicitly named traps with subtle concurrency/temporal semantics (idempotency replay incl. cached errors and same-key serialization, webhook retry/backoff/re-signing, PaymentIntent state machine), all offline against an external contract the agent must reconstruct. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep research of the real Stripe contract, milestone decomposition across a large surface, SDK-driven verification, progress tracking, and course-correction when compatibility breaks.

dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment
dimensions.description: Understanding the externally-defined Stripe wire contract (resource shapes, error codes, test PANs, list/idempotency/webhook semantics) and the SDK's expectations before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is really the real Stripe API; fidelity is graded against SDK behavior the agent must infer, not against this prose. Guessing field names, error codes, or the test-PAN set produces silently non-compliant output.

anchors.0: Starts coding straight from the prompt; invents field names, error codes, and PANs with no reference to actual Stripe behavior.
anchors.3: Recalls a few Stripe shapes from memory; covers the obvious resources but leaves error envelope, list envelope, or PAN set half-guessed.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error `{type,code,...}` mapping, list envelope, the published test-PAN set — and confirms how the SDK sets `api_base`/auth headers before building on them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract for the hard parts too: idempotency key scope `(api_key, key, body)`, webhook signature format, PaymentIntent status transitions, restricted-key scopes — grounded in how the real API/SDK behaves, and revisits sources as gaps surface mid-build.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-correcting reconstruction: cross-checks each subsystem's behavior against concrete SDK round-trips or documented Stripe semantics, catches under-specified corners (decline_code vs code, replay of cached error bodies, re-signing for replay windows) early, and lets findings reshape the design rather than discovering mismatches late.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered hierarchy — auth/boot skeleton, CRUD resources, then the risk-heavy idempotency/webhook/state-machine subsystems — each with a clear done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is too large to hold in one push, and the three named traps carry most of the risk; a flat, breadth-first slog will run out of horizon before the hard semantics are correct.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between endpoints ad hoc with no ordering or done-conditions.
anchors.3: A flat endpoint checklist with no risk prioritization and no explicit 'done' criteria per item.
anchors.5: Clear milestones (boot+auth first, then resource groups, then the traps) with rough done-conditions, and recognizes the three traps as distinct workstreams.
anchors.8: Risk-aware sequencing: gets a bootable auth'd skeleton verifiable early, then deliberately front-loads or ring-fences the high-risk subsystems (idempotency serialization, webhook backoff/re-sign, PI state machine) as first-class milestones each with an explicit check, rather than burying them in CRUD.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that visibly de-risks the whole horizon: dependencies made explicit (e.g. PaymentIntent charges before refunds before subscription invoices), the trickiest semantics scheduled while budget remains, and the plan carries concrete acceptance conditions per milestone that later verification maps onto.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how correctness is confirmed — exercising routes with the real `stripe` SDK / requests, and building targeted checks for idempotency, webhook retry, and state-machine edge cases — beyond 'it returns 200'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Wire-level compatibility and the trap semantics fail silently; only active verification (ideally through the SDK the way the verifier will) distinguishes a plausible-looking response from a compliant one.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because the code was written.
anchors.3: Manual curl of a couple of happy paths; no SDK check, no coverage of error bodies or the trap behaviors.
anchors.5: Boots the service, smoke-tests health and several CRUD flows, and checks a few error/edge cases — but leaves the hardest semantics (concurrent idempotent retries, webhook backoff, illegal state transitions) largely unverified.
anchors.8: Verifies through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and constructs specific checks for the traps: replaying an idempotency key (incl. a cached error body), same-key-different-body → 400, capturing a succeeded intent → 400, invalid PAN → decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff.
anchors.10: A deliberate verification harness that covers happy paths, error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, list pagination, restricted-key 403s, and the concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charge, re-signed late webhook deliveries), re-run after changes so regressions are caught rather than assumed away.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture over 12+ resource families and the trap subsystems, and detecting when effort is stuck or circling on one behavior.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing customers while subscriptions/invoices/webhooks remain unstarted, or re-debugging the same idempotency case repeatedly.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; forgets whole resource families or repeats work.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; discovers late that major endpoints or the webhook worker were never implemented.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and their status, and generally knows what remains.
anchors.8: Actively maintains coverage against the full route table, notices when stuck on one behavior and time-boxes it, and reallocates attention so no major area is silently dropped.
anchors.10: Continuous, accurate accounting across the whole horizon: distinguishes implemented-and-verified from implemented-only from missing, catches thrashing/circular debugging early and names it, and adjusts pace to land the full surface plus the traps within budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when SDK round-trips, error shapes, or trap semantics diverge from expectations — rather than pressing on with a falsified assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reconstructing an external contract guarantees wrong initial assumptions (field names, signature scheme, state rules); the agent must let contradicting evidence rewrite the design, sometimes structurally (e.g. how idempotency serialization or the billing worker is built).

anchors.0: Ignores failing SDK calls or wrong outputs; keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Patches surface symptoms (tweaks a field) without revisiting the underlying wrong model, so the same class of mismatch recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the root cause for that case and moves on.
anchors.8: Treats divergences as signals about the contract: on discovering e.g. a wrong signature format or state-transition rule, updates the mental model and propagates the fix across related endpoints, not just the one that failed.
anchors.10: Fluid, evidence-driven correction across the horizon, including structural pivots when needed (rethinking idempotency locking, webhook re-signing, or state-machine modeling once reality contradicts the plan), while preserving already-verified work — never barrels ahead on a falsified assumption.
